content: Electrocardiography (ECG or EKG, derived from the German term Elektrokardiogramm) is a non-invasive diagnostic tool that records the electrical activity of the heart over a period of time. This is achieved by placing electrodes on the skin's surface, which detect the heart's electrical signals. These signals are then recorded by an external device, producing a graphical representation known as an electrocardiogram (ECG or EKG). An ECG test measures the heart's electrical activity, including the rate and rhythm of heartbeats, the size and position of the heart chambers, the presence of any damage to the heart, and the effects of medications or devices like pacemakers. A standard 12-lead ECG records electrical signals from 12 different perspectives simultaneously, often printed as a paper copy for analysis. The ECG graph is plotted with time on the x-axis and voltage on the y-axis. At a paper speed of 25 mm/s, one small block on the ECG paper represents 40 milliseconds (ms), and five small blocks make up one large block, which corresponds to 200 ms. Therefore, there are five large blocks per second. The heart's electrical activity originates from the sinoatrial (SA) node, which initiates depolarization, leading to cardiac muscle contraction. This depolarization spreads in a specific sequence: from the SA node to the atria, then to the atrioventricular (AV) node (where conduction slows), followed by the bundle of His, the right and left bundle branches, and finally through the Purkinje fibers to the ventricles. The slowest conduction occurs at the AV node, causing a delay in the spread of electrical activity. A typical ECG tracing of the cardiac cycle includes the P wave, QRS complex, and T wave. The baseline voltage of the ECG is referred to as the isoelectric line. The P wave represents atrial depolarization. The QRS complex corresponds to ventricular depolarization and is larger than the P wave due to the greater muscular mass of the ventricles. The normal duration of the QRS complex is 120 ms (three small squares). If the first deflection is downward, it is called a Q wave. Any upward deflection is termed an R wave, regardless of whether it is preceded by a Q wave. A downward deflection following an R wave is called an S wave. The T wave represents ventricular repolarization. Atrial repolarization is not visible as it is buried within the QRS complex. The RR interval measures the time between successive R waves and reflects the regularity of the heart rhythm. A regular rhythm will have identical RR intervals throughout the ECG. The PR interval, measured from the beginning of the P wave to the start of the QRS complex, represents the time taken for the electrical impulse to travel from the sinus node through the AV node and into the ventricles. This interval is a good indicator of AV node function, with a normal duration of 120-200 ms (3-5 small squares). The PR segment connects the P wave and the QRS complex, but the PR interval is more clinically significant. The ST segment connects the QRS complex and the T wave, representing the period when the ventricles are depolarized. It is isoelectric. The electrical activity of the heart is measured using external electrodes placed on the skin. These electrodes are positioned at specific locations on the body to capture the heart's electrical signals. A total of 10 electrodes are used to derive 12 leads, which include six limb leads and six precordial leads. The four limb electrodes are: LA (left arm) RA (right arm) N (neutral, on the right leg, serving as the electrical ground) F (foot, on the left leg) The six chest electrodes are: V1: placed in the 4th intercostal space, right of the sternum V2: placed in the 4th intercostal space, left of the sternum V3: placed between V2 and V4 V4: placed in the 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line (under the breast in women) V5: placed between V4 and V6 V6: placed in the midaxillary line at the same horizontal level as V4 The term lead in electrocardiography can refer to either the electrical cable connecting the electrodes to the ECG recorder or the voltage difference between two electrodes, which is the actual tracing produced by the ECG recorder. For example, Lead I measures the voltage between the right arm and left arm electrodes, while Lead II measures the voltage between the right arm and the left leg. The leads provide different perspectives of the heart's electrical activity: Limb leads (I, II, III, aVL, aVR, aVF) view the heart in a vertical plane. Leads I and aVL focus on the left lateral side of the heart. Leads II, III, and aVF focus on the inferior side of the heart. Lead aVR focuses on the right atrium. Precordial (V) leads view the heart in a horizontal plane. V1 and V2 focus on the right ventricle. V3 and V4 focus on the septum and anterior wall of the left ventricle. V5 and V6 focus on the anterior and lateral walls of the left ventricle. The QRS complex shape varies across the precordial leads due to the direction of depolarization. Depolarization begins in the septum (left to right) and spreads to the ventricles. The left ventricular mass, being larger, directs the main electrical vector towards the left. In V1 and V2, septal depolarization produces an initial positive deflection (R wave) and a subsequent negative deflection (S wave). In V3 and V4, the QRS complex transitions to a predominantly positive deflection (R wave). The progression from V1 to V6 shows a gradual shift from a predominantly downward deflection in V1 to a predominantly upward deflection in V6. The transition point, where the R wave equals the S wave, indicates the position of the interventricular septum. In conditions like right ventricular hypertrophy, the septum may shift, altering the transition point to leads V5, V6, or even V7 instead of the usual V3 or V4. The overall direction of the heart's main electrical vector is from the right upper side to the left lower side, reflecting the sum of all depolarization waves.
